claim: At the onset of meiosis in starfish oocytes, a contractile F-actin network forms in the nuclear region transporting embedded chromosomes to the assembling microtubule spindle.
source: For example, at the onset of meiosis in starfish oocytes a contractile F-actin network forms in the nuclear region transporting embedded chromosomes to the assembling microtubule spindle.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a description of the biological system being studied.

claim: The F-actin network in starfish oocytes contracts homogeneously and isotropically mediating long-range and size-selective transport of chromosomes sterically trapped in the network.
source: It contracts homogeneously and isotropically mediating long-range and size-selective transport of chromosomes sterically trapped in the network.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction section, citing previous work (Mori et al., 2011).

claim: The initial contraction rate α0 of the F-actin network in starfish oocytes is 0.085 ± 0.017 min−1.
source: The value of α0 derived by this method from a large number of oocytes provided a precise estimate of the remarkably invariable initial contraction rate; α0 = 0.085 ± 0.017 min−1 (N = 53 ± S.D.).
evidence: This value is derived from experimental measurements of chromosome trajectories across 53 oocytes.

claim: Any pair of chromosomes exhibits a constant approach velocity towards one another during transport.
source: The trajectories revealed that any pair of chromosomes, irrespective of their initial location, exhibited a constant approach velocity towards one another during transport (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by linear fits to pair-wise distance measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Pair-wise chromosome velocities depend linearly on their initial separation distance.
source: Extrapolation of these linear trajectories showed that all chromosomes would meet at nearly the same time and location, if the network were to contract all the way to a single point (Figure 1C). This implies that pair-wise chromosome velocities depend linearly on their initial separation distance (Figure 1D), indicative of a spatially homogeneous and isotropic contraction (Mori et al., 2011).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D and is consistent with homogeneous isotropic contraction.

claim: New filaments are polymerized on nuclear envelope remnants (NER) forming a new network filling up the space around the contracting initial network.
source: Analysis of these pulse-label recordings revealed that while the network in the nuclear region contracts, new filaments are polymerized on nuclear envelope remnants (NER) forming a new network filling up the space around the contracting initial network (Figure 2A,C, Video 1).
evidence: This is observed through pulse-labeling experiments with phalloidin shown in Figure 2A and 2C.

claim: Polymerization occurs predominantly at the boundary defined by NER, and to a limited extent within the network.
source: Intensity profiles showed that polymerization occurred predominantly at the boundary defined by NER, and to a limited extent within the network (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by intensity profile analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The old network contracted to approximately half of its initial size with a nearly constant speed.
source: This revealed that the old network contracted to approximately half of its initial size, and with a nearly constant speed.
evidence: This is derived from measurements of the phalloidin-labeled network diameter over time.

claim: The network is under tension as evidenced by recoil response after laser ablation.
source: We observed a prominent recoil response with the network rapidly retracting away from the ablated region (Figure 3B–D, Video 2). This shows that the network is under tension and suggests that pushing by polymerization does not have a major contribution.
evidence: This is demonstrated by laser ablation experiments shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: High concentration of UtrCH effectively stabilized the network and prevented its contraction.
source: Similar to mouse oocytes (Holubcová et al., 2013), high concentration of UtrCH effectively stabilized the network and prevented its contraction (Figure 3B–D, Video 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B-D and is consistent with findings in mouse oocytes.

claim: F-actin mass within the old network continuously decreases through the contraction process.
source: Such quantifications extrapolated to the 3D volume revealed a continuous decrease of F-actin mass within the old network through the contraction process (Figure 4B, for F-actin densities see Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is measured by quantifying UtrCH fluorescence intensity as shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Both motor-driven and disassembly-driven models can recapitulate the observed contraction behavior.
source: We find that both models can recapitulate the observed behavior (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is shown by fitting both models to experimental data in Figure 4E.

claim: Perturbations of non-muscle myosin II have no effect on the rate of contraction.
source: To our surprise, these perturbations did not affect contraction rates derived from pair-wise chromosome approach (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with blebbistatin, MRLC overexpression, ML-7, and Y-27632 shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Blebbistatin treatment significantly decreased the amplitude of the contraction wave during polar body extrusion.
source: Consistent with our earlier results, the amplitude of the contraction wave was significantly decreased upon blebbistatin treatment, while it was increased in oocytes over-expressing MRLC (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C-D, confirming the effectiveness of the treatments.

claim: UtrCH slowed chromosome transport in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Analysis of pair-wise chromosome approach showed that UtrCH slowed chromosome transport in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 6A,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by titration experiments shown in Figure 6A and 6C.

claim: UtrCH slows net F-actin disassembly in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Analysis of F-actin mass in the old network revealed that UtrCH slows net F-actin disassembly in a dose-dependent manner (Table 2, Figure 6B,D).
evidence: This is shown by F-actin mass measurements in Figure 6B and 6D.

claim: Stabilization by UtrCH did not render the network denser or sparser, it merely slowed its contraction.
source: Quantification of changes in mean UtrCH intensity in a fixed size region on the other hand revealed similar F-actin density despite the very different contraction rates (Figure 6E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, respectively). In other words, stabilization by UtrCH did not render the network denser or sparser, it merely slowed its contraction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by density measurements shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The disassembly-driven model predicted contraction rates in response to gradual stabilization that matched experimental observations, while the motor-driven model did not.
source: For intermediate and high UtrCH levels, the motor-driven model predicted a fast increase of contraction rate, in contrast to the disassembly-driven model predicting contraction rate to remain nearly constant over time, well matching experimental observations (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is shown by model predictions compared to experimental data in Figure 6F.

claim: Latrunculin A treatment led to a dramatic increase in contraction rate approximately three-fold higher than DMSO controls.
source: We observed a dramatic increase in contraction rate upon acute treatment with a high dose of Latrunculin A (Figure 7A, Video 3). Starting approx. 50 s after Latrunculin A addition, the network diameter begun to decrease at rates approx. three-fold higher than DMSO controls (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments shown in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: The disassembly-driven model predicts an increase in contraction rate upon increased disassembly that closely matches experimentally observed values, while the motor-driven model does not.
source: While the motor-driven model predicted the contraction rate to change little upon increased disassembly, the disassembly-driven model predicts an increase in contraction rate closely matching experimentally observed values (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is shown by model predictions compared to Latrunculin A experimental data in Figure 7D.

claim: In the absence of molecular motors, a disassembling network with only cross-linkers did not contract over a broad range of parameters tested.
source: Consistent with previous theory and experiments (Belmonte et al., 2017; Bendix et al., 2008; Braun et al., 2016), in the absence of molecular motors the disassembling network did not contract over a broad range of parameters (number of filaments, cross-linkers and their unbinding rates) tested (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Cytosim simulations shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Introducing end-binding cross-linkers into the simulations resulted in robust large-scale contraction of the disassembling network in the absence of molecular motors.
source: Introducing such elements into the simulations, referred to as end-binding cross-linkers, resulted in robust large-scale contraction of the disassembling network in the absence of molecular motors (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Cytosim simulations shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Contraction rate is rather insensitive to the rate of filament assembly at the boundary.
source: Interestingly, we found that contraction rate is rather insensitive to the rate of filament assembly at the boundary: insufficient or excess filament production rates led to inhomogeneity in the network, but this did not significantly affect the rate of contraction (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulations testing different filament production rates shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The disassembly-driven mechanism invariably produces contraction with a constant speed, as observed experimentally, while motor-driven contraction typically accelerates.
source: First, the disassembly-driven mechanism invariably produces contraction with a constant speed, as observed experimentally, while motor-driven contraction typically accelerates (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is shown by comparing simulations of the two mechanisms in Figure 8C.

claim: Network density remains nearly constant during contraction in the disassembly-driven simulations, as in experiments, while during motor-driven contraction network density continuously increases.
source: Second, while a strictly quantitative comparison of the 2D simulations and the 3D experimental system is not possible, network density remains nearly constant during contraction in the disassembly-driven simulations, as in experiments, while during motor-driven contraction network density continuously increases (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is shown by comparing filament density in simulations in Figure 8D.

claim: Impairing formin activity with SMIFH2 led to a significant decrease of network contraction rate and a reduction of F-actin mass loss.
source: Impairing formin activity led to a significant decrease of network contraction rate and a reduction of F-actin mass loss, similar to stabilization by UtrCH, and well predicted by the disassembly-driven model (Figure 9E; Table 4 and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SMIFH2 treatment experiments shown in Figure 9.

claim: The F-actin network is essential to prevent formation of aneuploid eggs in starfish oocytes.
source: This F-actin network forms in the nuclear region after nuclear envelope breakdown (NEBD), at the onset of meiosis, and is essential to prevent formation of aneuploid eggs (Mori et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction, citing previous work (Mori et al., 2011).

claim: Connections of the network to the cell cortex provide directionality, resulting in transport towards the microtubule spindle located at the cortex.
source: While the contraction of the network is isotropic and homogeneous, connections of the network to the cell cortex provide directionality, resulting in transport towards the microtubule spindle, located at the cortex (Mori et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction, citing previous work (Mori et al., 2011).

claim: The reciprocal of α0, t0 = 1/α0 = 11.76 ± 0.27 min, is the 'convergence time', the time that would be required to transport the chromosomes from their initial position to the final meeting point.
source: Note that the reciprocal of this value, t0 = 1/α0= 11.76 ± 0.27 min is the 'convergence time', the time that would be required to transport the chromosomes from their initial position to the final meeting point.
evidence: This is calculated from the measured α0 value.

claim: The contraction rate derived from phalloidin-labeled network diameter was similar, although somewhat lower than the rate α0 determined by tracking chromosomes.
source: The rate of contraction derived this way was similar, although somewhat lower than the rate α0 determined by tracking chromosomes (compare Figures 1F and 2E).
evidence: This is observed by comparing measurements from the two methods shown in Figures 1F and 2E.

claim: Phalloidin used to visualize the old network slightly slows contraction and increases variability, likely dependent on the amount of phalloidin injected.
source: Thus, similar contraction rates are derived by the two methods, however, it appears that phalloidin used to visualize the old network slightly slows contraction and increases variability, likely dependent on the amount of phalloidin injected.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the two measurement methods.

claim: After retraction from laser ablation, the gap did not close, but was filled progressively by F-actin suggesting that in response to the perturbation, filament assembly may occur throughout the network.
source: After retraction, the gap did not close, but was filled progressively by F-actin suggesting that in response to the perturbation, filament assembly may occur throughout the network (Figure 3B,D).
evidence: This is observed in laser ablation experiments shown in Figure 3B and 3D.

claim: The recoil response did not depend on the direction of the cut, consistent with isotropic contraction.
source: The recoil response did not depend on the direction of the cut, consistent with isotropic contraction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ablation experiments in different directions shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the motor-driven model, decreasing disassembly rate caused an increase in F-actin concentration that resulted in more effective motor action, leading to an increase of contraction rate over time.
source: This is explained by the fact that in the disassembly-driven mechanism contraction and disassembly rates are inherently coupled. In the motor-driven model, decreasing disassembly rate caused an increase in F-actin concentration that resulted in more effective motor action, leading to the observed increase of contraction rate over time.
evidence: This is an explanation of the model behavior based on the model equations.

claim: Latrunculin A is expected to block actin filament assembly and to enhance depolymerization by reducing the effective monomer concentration.
source: To further test the active role of disassembly in driving contraction, we used Latrunculin A, a toxin that sequesters actin monomers. Therefore, Latrunculin A is expected to block actin filament assembly and to enhance depolymerization by reducing the effective monomer concentration (Spector et al., 1989).
evidence: This is based on the known mechanism of Latrunculin A action, citing Spector et al., 1989.

claim: In a dynamically assembling and disassembling network, Latrunculin A shifts the equilibrium towards disassembly.
source: Thus, in a dynamically assembling and disassembling network the net effect will be shifting the equilibrium towards disassembly.
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanism of Latrunculin A action.

claim: Starting approximately 50 s after Latrunculin A addition, the network diameter begun to decrease at rates approximately three-fold higher than DMSO controls.
source: Starting approx. 50 s after Latrunculin A addition, the network diameter begun to decrease at rates approx. three-fold higher than DMSO controls (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is measured from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 7B.

claim: mDia1 is able to track depolymerizing ends and generate pulling forces on the disassembling filament end in vitro under specific conditions.
source: It has been shown that in vitro and under specific conditions the formin, mDia1 is able to track depolymerizing ends and generate pulling forces on the disassembling filament end (Jégou et al., 2013; Mizuno et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated based on previous in vitro studies cited.

claim: Formins have been shown to have cross-linking activities on their own or by binding to other actin regulators such as Spire.
source: In addition, formins have been shown to have cross-linking activities on their own or by binding to other actin regulators such as Spire (Esue et al., 2008; Montaville et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated based on previous studies cited.

claim: SMIFH2 is a small-molecule inhibitor of the FH2 domain contained and essential for the activity of all known formins.
source: We tested this hypothesis by inhibiting all formin-like activities in the oocyte by SMIFH2, a small-molecule inhibitor of the FH2 domain contained and essential for the activity of all known formins (Rizvi et al., 2009), and which has already been evaluated in mouse and starfish oocytes (Kim et al., 2015; Ucar et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated based on the known properties of SMIFH2, citing relevant studies.

claim: The meiotic spindle is small across animal species due to the requirement for highly asymmetric division in oocytes.
source: Oocytes also divide very asymmetrically in order to retain these nutrients in a single egg. The requirement for this highly asymmetric division constrains the size of the meiotic spindle. Therefore, across animal species, the meiotic spindle is small and this necessitates additional mechanism to collect and transport chromosomes scattered in the large nuclear volume to the forming microtubule spindle.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an explanation for the need for chromosome transport mechanisms.

claim: The process is triggered by NEBD opening the previously inaccessible nuclear compartment to cytoplasmic actin, actin assembly factors and cross-linkers resulting in the rapid assembly of a cross-linked F-actin network in the nuclear region.
source: First, the process is triggered by NEBD opening the previously inaccessible nuclear compartment to cytoplasmic actin, actin assembly factors and cross-linkers resulting in the rapid assembly of a cross-linked F-actin network in the nuclear region.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as part of the proposed mechanism.

claim: The disassembling network will eventually release the transported chromosomes, as it loses connectivity and stops contracting.
source: Finally, an additional elegant feature of the system is that the disassembling network will eventually release the transported chromosomes, as it loses connectivity and stops contracting.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a predicted feature of the disassembly-driven mechanism.

claim: In the absence of disassembly, a contracting network would necessarily densify, in which case the chromosomes would be surrounded by a tight meshwork of F-actin at the end of contraction, which would likely interfere with their capture by spindle microtubules.
source: By contrast, in the absence of disassembly, a contracting network would necessarily densify, in which case the chromosomes would be surrounded by a tight meshwork of F-actin at the end of contraction, which would likely interfere with their capture by spindle microtubules.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a contrast to the disassembly-driven mechanism.

claim: Network contraction can be seen as a large-scale treadmilling system, where F-actin disassembles in bulk and is replenished by filaments polymerized at the NER boundary.
source: Network contraction can be seen here as a large-scale treadmilling system, where F-actin disassembles in bulk and is replenished by filaments polymerized at the NER boundary.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as an interpretation of the mechanism.

claim: De-novo filament assembly at the NER boundary does not participate in force generation, which rather originates in the bulk of the network.
source: However, the evidences lead us to conclude that de-novo filament assembly at the NER boundary does not participate in force generation, which rather originates in the bulk of the network.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion from the experimental and simulation results.

claim: Actin polymerization is well established to produce force at cell protrusions.
source: While actin polymerization is well established to produce force, at cell protrusions, for example (Footer et al., 2007; Krause and Gautreau, 2014), force production by disassembly has so far only been evidenced in vitro for specific actin concentration (Jégou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated based on established knowledge and cited studies.

claim: Force production by disassembly has so far only been evidenced in vitro for specific actin concentration.
source: While actin polymerization is well established to produce force, at cell protrusions, for example (Footer et al., 2007; Krause and Gautreau, 2014), force production by disassembly has so far only been evidenced in vitro for specific actin concentration (Jégou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated based on cited in vitro studies.

claim: Microtubule depolymerization can produce force that is harnessed to drive separation of sister chromatids in anaphase.
source: It is clear that microtubule depolymerization can produce force (Grishchuk et al., 2005), that is harnessed for example to drive separation of sister chromatids in anaphase (Cheeseman and Desai, 2008; Westermann et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated based on established knowledge and cited studies.

claim: Actin polymerization is tightly coupled to nucleotide hydrolysis driving the system out of equilibrium that may enable generation of force by depolymerization.
source: Similar to tubulin, actin polymerization is tightly coupled to nucleotide hydrolysis driving the system out of equilibrium that may enable generation of force by depolymerization (Braun et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a possible mechanism, citing Braun et al., 2016.

claim: Entropic forces generated either by crowding agents surrounding filaments or by diffusible cross-linkers confined in filament overlaps could drive contraction.
source: Alternatively, entropic forces generated either by crowding agents surrounding filaments or by diffusible cross-linkers confined in filament overlaps could drive contraction (Braun et al., 2016), but we have not tested this possibility.
evidence: This is stated as an alternative possibility that was not tested, citing Braun et al., 2016.

claim: SMIFH2 has been shown to inhibit formins in starfish oocytes, but its specificity and selectivity profile is yet to be characterized.
source: These results need to be confirmed, since they rely on a small-molecule inhibitor, SMIFH2, which has been shown to inhibit formins in starfish oocytes (Ucar et al., 2013), but its specificity and selectivity profile is yet to be characterized.
evidence: This is stated as a caveat regarding the SMIFH2 experiments, citing Ucar et al., 2013.

claim: The observed effect of SMIFH2 may be indirect resulting from the altered balance between other formin-driven actin assembly pathways and Arp2/3 nucleated structures.
source: Secondly, the observed effect may be indirect resulting from the altered balance between other formin-driven actin assembly pathways and Arp2/3 nucleated structures, as recently showed in yeast (Burke et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as an alternative explanation for the SMIFH2 effects, citing Burke et al., 2014.

claim: Mouse oocytes feature a dynamic cytoplasmic F-actin network required to position the nucleus.
source: For example, mouse oocytes feature a dynamic cytoplasmic F-actin network required to position the nucleus (Almonacid et al., 2015), the meiotic spindle (Almonacid et al., 2014; Azoury et al., 2008; Schuh and Ellenberg, 2008), and to transport vesicles from the cell center to the cortex, including cortical granules to prevent polyspermy (Cheeseman et al., 2016; Schuh, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction, citing multiple studies on mouse oocytes.

claim: Myosin II and myosin V motors have been involved in transporting the spindle and vesicles, respectively, in mouse oocytes.
source: While myosin II and myosin V motors have been involved in transporting the spindle and vesicles, respectively, filament dynamics appear to have a key role in these processes as well, regulated by Fmn2/Spire1/2 as well as cortical Arp2/3 nucleators, and other factors (Chaigne et al., 2013; Cheeseman et al., 2016; Holubcová et al., 2013; Pfender et al., 2011; Schuh, 2011; Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction, citing multiple studies on mouse oocytes.

claim: Filament dynamics appear to have a key role in spindle and vesicle transport in mouse oocytes, regulated by Fmn2/Spire1/2 as well as cortical Arp2/3 nucleators, and other factors.
source: While myosin II and myosin V motors have been involved in transporting the spindle and vesicles, respectively, filament dynamics appear to have a key role in these processes as well, regulated by Fmn2/Spire1/2 as well as cortical Arp2/3 nucleators, and other factors (Chaigne et al., 2013; Cheeseman et al., 2016; Holubcová et al., 2013; Pfender et al., 2011; Schuh, 2011; Yu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction, citing multiple studies.

claim: The mechanism of contractile force generation is well understood in sarcomeric-like assemblies, such as muscles or stress fibers.
source: Generally, while the mechanism of contractile force generation is well understood in sarcomeric-like assemblies, such as muscles or stress fibers, the mechanisms in disordered F-actin networks, such as the above quasi-2D cortical and 3D cytoplasmic networks, remains much more elusive (Lenz et al., 2012; Murrell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as established knowledge, citing reviews.

claim: The mechanisms of contractile force generation in disordered F-actin networks remains much more elusive.
source: Generally, while the mechanism of contractile force generation is well understood in sarcomeric-like assemblies, such as muscles or stress fibers, the mechanisms in disordered F-actin networks, such as the above quasi-2D cortical and 3D cytoplasmic networks, remains much more elusive (Lenz et al., 2012; Murrell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction, citing reviews.

claim: Computational models and theoretical work so far focused largely on disordered F-actin networks formed by non-dynamic filaments inspired by in vitro reconstituted contractile systems composed of stable filaments.
source: Additionally, computational models and theoretical work so far focused largely on disordered F-actin networks formed by non-dynamic filaments inspired by in vitro reconstituted contractile systems composed of stable filaments (Alvarado and Koenderink, 2015; Belmonte et al., 2017; Bendix et al., 2008; Köhler and Bausch, 2012; Murrell and Gardel, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction, citing multiple studies.

claim: Theoretical work has shown that F-actin dynamics is able to generate not only protrusive but also contractile stress.
source: Indeed, although much less investigated, theoretical work has shown that F-actin dynamics is able to generate not only protrusive but also contractile stress (Sun et al., 2010; Zumdieck et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction, citing theoretical studies.

claim: Cell migration is to a large part driven by polymerization of actin filaments at the cell front and depolymerization at the rear.
source: For example, cell migration is to a large part driven by polymerization of actin filaments at the cell front and depolymerization at the rear (Cramer, 2013; Mseka and Cramer, 2011; Pollard and Borisy, 2003; Ridley, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as established knowledge, citing multiple studies.

claim: Cytokinetic ring closure has been shown to be driven by depolymerization of filaments in some species, although myosin activity certainly is the main driver in others.
source: Cytokinetic ring closure has been shown to be driven by depolymerization of filaments in some species, although myosin activity certainly is the main driver in others (Green et al., 2012; Mendes Pinto et al., 2012; Neujahr et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction, citing studies on different species.

claim: Non-muscle myosin II is the main driver of cortical processes including cell migration, cell division and tissue morphogenesis.
source: While myosin motor activity, non-muscle myosin II in particular, is the main driver of these processes, filament dynamics has been shown to play a critical role as well.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as established knowledge.

claim: The cortex, a thin and entangled network of F-actin underlying the plasma membrane determines the shape of animal cells.
source: Most prominently, the cortex, a thin and entangled network of F-actin underlying the plasma membrane determines the shape of animal cells, and changes in cell shape underlie cell migration, cell division and tissue morphogenesis (Munjal and Lecuit, 2014; Pollard and Cooper, 2009; Salbreux et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction as established knowledge, citing reviews.

claim: Recent studies revealed extensive 3D F-actin networks in the bulk cytoplasm of large oocytes and embryos with essential functions in intracellular transport processes.
source: In addition to its cortical functions, recent studies revealed extensive 3D F-actin networks in the bulk cytoplasm of large oocytes and embryos with essential functions in intracellular transport processes (Field and Lénárt, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction, citing a review.

claim: Observations are well explained by models based on a disassembly-driven contractile mechanism.
source: We found no evidence of myosin activity driving network contractility. Instead, our observations are well explained by models based on a disassembly-driven contractile mechanism.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract as a main conclusion of the study.

claim: No evidence of myosin activity driving network contractility was found.
source: We found no evidence of myosin activity driving network contractility.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract as a main finding of the study.

claim: The disassembly-based contractile system robustly drives chromosome transport to prevent aneuploidy in the large oocyte, a prerequisite for normal embryonic development.
source: We reconstitute this disassembly-based contractile system in silico revealing a simple architecture that robustly drives chromosome transport to prevent aneuploidy in the large oocyte, a prerequisite for normal embryonic development.
evidence: This is stated in the Abstract as a main conclusion of the study.
